newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FOCUS-Brazil Central Bank president resigns.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Brazil Central Bank president resigns.

text.p: The head of Brazil's Central Bank, Gustavo Loyola, will resign and its international affairs director, Gustavo Franco, has been nominated to take his place, Finance Minister Pedro Malan said Tuesday.
"Gustavo Loyola is leaving the presidency of the Central Bank," Malan told reporters.
Franco's appointment as Central Bank president must be confirmed by the Senate.
Malan said it was "premature" to name a replacement for the international affairs director, who controls Brazilian foreign exchange policy and presides over its overseas debt issues.
But the minister stressed that whoever took over would maintain current policies.
"There will not be any change in economic policy. It is an absolute waste of time to speculate if the person who will take over from Gustavo Franco will change policy," Malan said.
Loyola, who attended the news conference with Malan, said he was stepping down because he believed he had completed his stated task of presiding over the reconstruction of Brazil's financial system.

Known to have felt uncomfortable in the limelight of the Central Bank presidency and often under attack from Congress, Loyola said he did not know what he would do next. He said he had offered his services as a consultant to the government.

"Despite leaving the bank, I will continue to contribute as long as it's in the interests of the minister (Malan), to contribute to the reconstruction of the financial system. There is still a lot of work there," Loyola said.
Political analysts concurred with Malan's view that little would change.

"This had been expected for a long time although the speculation had died off a bit. He (Loyola) was an important player but not a decisive one," Murillo Aragao of Brasilia consultants Arko Advice said.
Under Loyola, the Brazilian Central Bank helped guide the banking sector through the transition from hyperinflation to a stable economy, though the bank's performance was at times criticized.

The government's PROER program of cheap credit lines for mergers and acquisitions has helped shrink the overcrowded banking system, herding some of the weaker institutions into the hands of the more able.

Franco and Loyola are both credited with overseeing the success so far of Brazil's "Plano Real" economic stabilization plan, which has brought chronic hyperinflation down to about 10 percent last year.
Loyola, aged 44, joined the Central Bank in 1977 and apart from odd spells in the private sector as a consultant or professor, spent most of his career in the institution.
Franco, who in particular is identified as one of the "fathers" of the Plano Real, joined the government four years ago.
Loyola will remain at the helm of the Central Bank until Franco's nomination has been approved by the Senate.
